questions.q: For a 200-task, 1,000-shot-per-task job, what is the total AWS Braket cost on IonQ Aria ($0.30/task + $0.03/shot) versus Rigetti Ankaa-3 ($0.30/task + $0.0009/shot)?
options: Both devices cost exactly $240.00, since the per-task fee is identical
IonQ Aria: $240.00; Rigetti Ankaa-3: $6,060.00
Both cost $6,060.00, since shot count is the same for both
IonQ Aria: $6,060.00; Rigetti Ankaa-3: $240.00 -- roughly a 25x difference for the identical workload
questions.explain: IonQ Aria: 200x$0.30 + 200,000x$0.03 = $60+$6,000 = $6,060. Rigetti Ankaa-3: 200x$0.30 + 200,000x$0.0009 = $60+$180 = $240. The per-shot fee difference drives a roughly 25x total cost difference.

questions.q: Why can't you directly compare an AWS Braket cost quote (based on shots and tasks) against an IBM Quantum Pay-As-You-Go quote using the same shot-count-based formula?
options: IBM bills by runtime seconds, not shots or tasks -- estimating IBM cost requires estimating wall-clock execution time, which depends on circuit depth and queueing behavior, not shot count directly
IBM only accepts jobs priced in a foreign currency
Braket and IBM actually use the exact same pricing formula
IBM Quantum doesn't charge for quantum computing at all
questions.explain: Braket's cost scales with (tasks, shots), while IBM's Pay-As-You-Go cost scales with billable runtime seconds -- a fundamentally different pricing dimension requiring a different estimation approach, as covered in the provider APIs lesson.

questions.q: In the verified AWS program-sets example (100 circuits x 1,000 shots on Rigetti Ankaa-3), what specifically produces the $29.70 savings when using a program set?
options: Program sets eliminate shot costs entirely
A reduced per-shot price when using program sets
Paying the $0.30 per-task fee once instead of 100 times, while the per-shot cost stays identical either way
A volume discount applied to the entire bill, including shots
questions.explain: Without program sets: 100x$0.30 + 100,000x$0.0009 = $120.00. With program sets: 1x$0.30 + 100,000x$0.0009 = $90.30. The $29.70 difference is exactly 99x$0.30 -- the eliminated redundant per-task fees, not a change in per-shot pricing.

questions.q: In the lesson's pricing table, OQC Lucy is the cheapest device for the 200-task example at $130.00. Why does the lesson caution against automatically choosing the cheapest device?
options: Qubit count/connectivity, native gate error rates, and queue depth also matter -- a cheaper device might not fit the circuit, might be too noisy to produce a useful answer, or might have a queue long enough to cost more in total project time
Cheaper devices are illegal to use for production workloads
Cost is the only factor that ever matters in backend selection
OQC Lucy is actually always the most expensive device in practice
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists qubit count/connectivity, error rate, and queue depth (tying back to Chapter 3's latency discussion) as additional factors that can make a 'cheaper' device the wrong overall choice once total cost and usability are considered.

questions.q: A 50-task, 2,000-shot job on IonQ Harmony ($0.30/task + $0.01/shot) costs how much without program-set batching, and how much with it?
options: Without: $15.00. With: $0.30 (shots are not billed in this example)
Without: $1,000.30. With: $1,015.00 (program sets increase cost)
Both cases cost exactly $1,000.00 with no difference
questions.explain: Without batching: 50x$0.30 + (50x2,000)x$0.01 = $15 + $1,000 = $1,015.00. With program-set batching, the per-task fee is paid once: $0.30 + $1,000 = $1,000.30, saving $14.70 (49x$0.30, the eliminated redundant per-task fees).
